abstract: Speech and music engage overlapping auditory cortex. We asked whether they shape the timing of local activity in ways that regional response strength alone leaves unresolved. In intracranial recordings from 30 participants watching a film with alternating music and speech, 1-10-Hz activity in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) had higher sample entropy during music, indicating that similar short patterns were less likely to persist (mean paired difference = 0.02256, FDR q = 0.00753). The contrast persisted in comparisons of adjacent film blocks and was larger relative to surrogate signals matched for amplitude distribution and approximate power spectrum. Speech elicited higher STG high-frequency power in the intracranial subset and stronger bilateral STG BOLD responses in all 30 participants in the separately acquired fMRI recordings. Together, these findings show that the soundtrack category associated with stronger regional responses differs from the one associated with greater local temporal irregularity. The temporal organisation of local activity therefore adds a dimension to how shared auditory cortex responds to natural sounds.
